title: Supreme Court won't weigh in on doctor bias training
text:

 A lawyer for the physician challenging the training said it sends a damaging message about hidden racial prejudices.
 Maureen Groppe USA TODAY Updated Nov. 16, 2026, 10:16 a.m. ET Hear this story WASHINGTON – The Supreme Cour t won't decide whether requiring doctors to be educated about implicit biases that can affect health care delivery violates the First Amendment.
 The court on Nov. 16 rejected a challenge to California’s rule that continuing education programs address unconscious prejudices doctors may have about Black people, women and others.
 A lawyer for the physician challenging the rule said such training sends a damaging message.
 "It tells doctors that their colleagues harbor hidden racial prejudices that no amount of training can fully cure, and it tells minority patients that a white physician is likely to damage their health," Caleb Trotter, a senior attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation, said in a statement . "That’s not medicine. It’s compelled speech."
 Three of the court's most conservative justices − Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch − said they would have taken the case.
 It takes four justices to agree to hear an appeal.
 When adopting the implicit bias education requirement in 2019, the California legislature said unconscious prejudices often contribute to unequal health care based on a patient’s race, gender, age, disability or other characteristic.
 African Americans, for example, are often prescribed less pain medication than White patients with similar problems and women are less likely to survive a heart attack when treated by a male doctor, the legislature found.
 Lower courts dismissed the challenge from Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, whose first name means "freedom" in Farsi, the language of her home country of Iran. Khatibi’s family fled Tehran when she was six to escape repression, according to her lawyer.
 The California-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the continuing education classes are a form of government speech. While the First Amendment prevents the government from regulating private speech, it does not regulate government speech.
 And California has long controlled the practice of medicine, the court said, reflecting the state’s "evolving judgment" of essential knowledge for competent doctors, "of which implicit bias is one."
 Thomas, in explaining why he wanted to take the case, said the training requirement "is not speech by any government actor; it is a requirement that private speakers communicate certain messages."
 "We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as 'a cover for censorship' or a cloak forcompelled speech," Thomas wrote.
